# Problem 1
```{r}
data("ny_noaa")

noaa_missing =
  ny_noaa |>
  summarise(
    prop_prcp_na = mean(is.na(prcp)),
    prop_snow_na = mean(is.na(snow)),
    prop_snwd_na = mean(is.na(snwd)),
    prop_tmax_na = mean(is.na(tmax)),
    prop_tmin_na = mean(is.na(tmin))
  )
```
The `ny_noaa` dataset contains daily weather observations from `r n_distinct(ny_noaa$id)` New York state weather stations spanning from `r min(ny_noaa$date)` to `r max(ny_noaa$date)`, with `r format(nrow(ny_noaa), big.mark = ",")` rows and `r ncol(ny_noaa)` columns. Key variables include weather station identifier (`id`), observation date (`date`), precipitation in tenths of millimeters (`prcp`), snowfall in millimeters (`snow`), snow depth in millimeters (`snwd`), and maximum and minimum temperatures in tenths of degrees Celsius (`tmax` and `tmin`). Missing data is a substantial issue because many stations only record a subset of meteorological variables: `tmax` and `tmin` are each missing in `r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * noaa_missing$prop_tmax_na)` and `r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * noaa_missing$prop_tmin_na)` of observations, `snwd` is missing in `r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * noaa_missing$prop_snwd_na)`, `snow` is missing in `r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * noaa_missing$prop_snow_na)`, and `prcp` is missing in `r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * noaa_missing$prop_prcp_na)`.

```{r}
noaa_df =
  ny_noaa |>
  separate(
    date,
    into = c("year", "month", "day"),
    sep = "-",
    convert = TRUE
  ) |>
  mutate(
    prcp = prcp / 10,
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10
  )

snow_top =
  noaa_df |>
  filter(!is.na(snow)) |>
  count(snow, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 5)

kable(
  snow_top,
  col.names = c("Snowfall (mm)", "Observations"),
  caption = "Top 5 Most Commonly Observed Snowfall Values"
)
```

I separated `date` into integer `year`, `month`, and `day` variables, and converted `prcp` from tenths of millimeters to millimeters (`mm`) as well as `tmax` and `tmin` from tenths of degrees Celsius to degrees Celsius (`°C`), so that precipitation, snowfall, and snow depth are all measured in `mm` and temperatures in `°C`. For snowfall, the most commonly observed value is `0` mm (`r format(snow_top$n[1], big.mark = ",")` observations), because snow does not fall on the vast majority of days across the year in New York State. The next most common values are `25` mm, `13` mm, `51` mm, and `76` mm, which correspond to historical measurements recorded in imperial inches (1.0 inch = 25.4 mm, 0.5 inch = 12.7 mm, 2.0 inches = 50.8 mm, and 3.0 inches = 76.2 mm) and subsequently rounded to the nearest millimeter.

```{r}
jan_july_tmax =
  noaa_df |>
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7), !is.na(tmax)) |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(
      month,
      levels = c(1, 7),
      labels = c("January", "July")
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarise(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(jan_july_tmax, aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.15, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, size = 0.8, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = 1), color = "firebrick", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  labs(
    title = "Station-Level Average Maximum Temperature in January and July (1981-2010)",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average Maximum Temperature (°C)"
  )
```

The two-panel plot shows a clear seasonal separation: average maximum temperatures in January generally fluctuate between -10 °C and 10 °C (centered near 0 °C), whereas July average maximum temperatures stay much warmer and more tightly clustered between 20 °C and 32 °C (centered near 27 °C). Across stations, year-to-year fluctuations move in parallel, reflecting statewide warm and cold years. Several notable outliers appear in both panels, most prominently an abnormally cold July station-year observation in 1988 (`USC00308962` at 13.95 °C) and an extremely cold January station-year observation in 1982 (`USC00301723` at -13.44 °C).

```{r fig.height=8}
tmax_tmin_plot =
  noaa_df |>
  filter(!is.na(tmax), !is.na(tmin)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_hex(bins = 50) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Count", trans = "log10") +
  labs(
    title = "(i) Daily Maximum vs. Minimum Temperature",
    x = "Minimum Temperature (°C)",
    y = "Maximum Temperature (°C)"
  )

snow_dist_plot =
  noaa_df |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  mutate(year = factor(year)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = snow, y = year, fill = after_stat(x))) +
  geom_density_ridges_gradient(scale = 2.2, rel_min_height = 0.01) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Snowfall (mm)", option = "C") +
  labs(
    title = "(ii) Snowfall Distribution (0 < Snow < 100 mm) by Year",
    x = "Snowfall (mm)",
    y = "Year"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

tmax_tmin_plot / snow_dist_plot
```

In panel (i), a hexagonal heatmap of `tmax` versus `tmin` avoids severe overplotting across over 1.46 million complete pairs and reveals a tight positive linear relationship, with the highest density of daily observations concentrated between `tmin` of -5 °C to 15 °C and `tmax` of 5 °C to 25 °C. In panel (ii), the yearly ridge density plots of snowfall values between 0 and 100 mm remain remarkably consistent across all 30 years and exhibit distinct multimodal peaks near 13 mm, 25 mm, 51 mm, and 76 mm, further confirming the unit-conversion rounding from quarter-, half-, and whole-inch snowfall recordings.

# Problem 2
```{r}
covar_raw =
  read_csv(
    "data/nhanes_covar.csv",
    skip = 4,
    na = c("", "NA"),
    col_types = cols(
      SEQN = col_integer(),
      sex = col_integer(),
      age = col_double(),
      BMI = col_double(),
      education = col_integer()
    )
  ) |>
  clean_names()

accel_raw =
  read_csv(
    "data/nhanes_accel.csv",
    col_types = cols(
      .default = col_double(),
      SEQN = col_integer()
    )
  ) |>
  clean_names()

covar_df =
  covar_raw |>
  filter(age >= 21) |>
  drop_na(seqn, sex, age, bmi, education) |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(
      sex,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c("Male", "Female")
    ),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c(
        "Less than high school",
        "High school equivalent",
        "More than high school"
      ),
      ordered = TRUE
    )
  )

nhanes_wide =
  covar_df |>
  inner_join(accel_raw, by = "seqn")

nhanes_long =
  nhanes_wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("min"),
    names_to = "minute",
    names_prefix = "min",
    names_transform = list(minute = as.integer),
    values_to = "mims"
  )
```

I skipped the first four metadata lines when importing `nhanes_covar.csv`, standardized column names, excluded participants younger than 21 years old (`r sum(covar_raw$age < 21, na.rm = TRUE)` participants) and those with missing demographic values (`r nrow(covar_raw) - sum(covar_raw$age < 21, na.rm = TRUE) - nrow(covar_df)` participants), and encoded `sex` and `education` as ordered factors. Merging with the accelerometer file yielded `r nrow(nhanes_wide)` eligible participants across `r ncol(nhanes_wide)` variables in wide format, and `r format(nrow(nhanes_long), big.mark = ",")` participant-minute observations in tidy long format.

```{r}
edu_sex_table =
  covar_df |>
  count(education, sex) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n
  )

kable(
  edu_sex_table,
  col.names = c("Education Level", "Male", "Female"),
  caption = "Number of Men and Women in Each Education Category"
)

ggplot(covar_df, aes(x = education, y = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.6, width = 0.5, position = position_dodge(0.75), outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(aes(color = sex), position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.15, dodge.width = 0.75), alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Age Distributions by Sex and Education Level",
    x = "Education Level",
    y = "Age (Years)",
    fill = "Sex",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```

The largest subgroup is participants with more than a high school education (56 men and 59 women), with balanced sex counts in both the "Less than high school" (27 men, 28 women) and "More than high school" categories, whereas men outnumber women in the "High school equivalent" group (35 men vs. 23 women). The age distribution plot indicates that participants in the "More than high school" group are substantially younger overall (especially women, whose median age is around 41 years) compared with the other two education categories. In the "High school equivalent" category, women tend to be older than men, while in "Less than high school" both men and women skew toward older ages (median near 60 years).

```{r}
total_activity_df =
  nhanes_long |>
  group_by(seqn, sex, age, bmi, education) |>
  summarise(
    total_activity = sum(mims, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(total_activity_df, aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.65) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Daily Physical Activity vs. Age by Sex and Education Level",
    x = "Age (Years)",
    y = "Total Daily Activity (Sum of MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```

Across all three education levels, total daily physical activity declines steadily with advancing age. In the "Less than high school" group, men and women exhibit comparable activity levels with a steep decline after age 60, whereas in both the "High school equivalent" and "More than high school" groups, women consistently record higher average total daily MIMS values than men of the same age. Additionally, participants in the "High school equivalent" category show a pronounced peak in total activity around ages 35 to 45 before declining at older ages.


```{r}
hourly_activity_plot =
  nhanes_long |>
  ggplot(aes(x = minute / 60, y = mims, color = sex)) +
  geom_line(
    stat = "summary",
    fun = mean,
    alpha = 0.35,
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.1) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 24, by = 4)) +
  labs(
    title = "24-Hour Physical Activity Profiles by Education Level and Sex",
    x = "Hour of Day (from Midnight)",
    y = "Activity Level (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  )

hourly_activity_plot
```

The 24-hour activity profiles follow a distinct circadian rhythm across all three education groups: activity drops to its lowest level during overnight sleeping hours (between midnight and 5:00 AM), rises sharply between 6:00 AM and 9:00 AM, remains elevated throughout the daytime (9:00 AM to 6:00 PM), and tapers off steadily during the evening. In the "High school equivalent" and "More than high school" panels, women maintain noticeably higher daytime MIMS levels than men from mid-morning through early evening, whereas in the "Less than high school" group, men and women track closely throughout the day with slightly higher midday peaks among men.
